title: R' Yosi ben Pazi
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: In his account of the Zohar, Lekh (in Sitrei Torah), 88b, Hyman relates that R' Abba, when he came from there, proclaimed: whoever desires wealth or length of days, let him come and exert himself in Torah. There came to him one named Yose, who told him that he wished to study in order to become rich. [R' Abba] told his disciples to call R' Yose "master of wealth." After he had studied much, he came to R' Abba to ask for the wealth that [R' Abba] had promised him — then a certain very rich man came with much gold and said to R' Abba, "I wish to merit [a share] in Torah, and I have not merited it; therefore, if someone will study on my behalf, I will give him my silver and my gold." R' Abba ordered that his wealth be given to this R' Yose. But afterward, following a remarkable incident, he returned to R' Abba and wept that he had taken money in exchange for his Torah, and he distributed his wealth to the poor and to orphans. Because of this they called him Rabbi Yose ben Pazi (from the word paz, pure gold). So too it is mentioned in the Midrash ha-Ne'elam on Genesis, the passage beginning “Let the earth bring forth”, and there in Lekh 88b.

notes.text: This physical notice is retained separately from other notices with the same heading; no identity between them is asserted. Hyman derives Pazi from paz, pure gold. The Zohar reference was not independently confirmed: the named public request failed. The particular “remarkable incident” remains unspecified.

Two whole saved Vocalized Zohar, Israel 2013, Lech Lecha scalars at versions[0].text[25][16] (481 chars) and [25][15] (341 chars) were read with raw SHA256, exact selectors, scalar hashes and actual edition metadata checked. The conclusion explicitly names Rabbi Yose ben Pazi, supporting Rabbi only for the final p002 naming clause. The heading, p001, earlier abbreviated Yose occurrences, and every Abba abbreviation remain R'; the selected scalars call the teacher his master or leave the speaker implicit, without supplying the name Abba or licensing a full-title transfer to those earlier occurrences. The current title's Yosi and the body Yose remain distinct transliterations. These two selected scalars show love of Torah entering him, his tears and speech about the world to come, the instruction to the other man to give wealth to orphans and the poor, and Rabbi Yose returning the cup of paz. Hyman instead compresses the intervening event as a remarkable incident and says he distributed his wealth to the poor and orphans; those source words and ordering remain translated without silently replacing the donor, resolving compressed pronouns, or importing the cup, world-to-come speech, descendants or reward into the body. The longer proclamation and earlier exchange were not selected as whole primary evidence here. The source's claim that Yose studied to become rich, its direct first-person wish and conditional gift of my silver and my gold, the promised wealth and dash, and the derivation from paz remain intact. The named digital response is not proof of Hyman's 88b folio mapping, Sitrei Torah subheading, printed spelling or correction history; the separate Midrash ha-Ne'elam Genesis passage beginning Let the earth bring forth remains unchecked. The consulted scan of Hyman II, p. 734, preserves this separate notice and its Lekh 88b reference; it is not merged with another notice bearing the same heading. All six connected selected Zohar Lech Lecha passages were read, including the earlier proclamation and exchange. They explicitly name Rabbi Abba and locally give the young man the name Rabbi Yose, but that evidence is not transferred to unrelated occurrences or the heading. The proclamation specifies length of days in the world to come, whereas Hyman abbreviates it to length of days. The rich man carries a vessel or cup of fine gold and describes inherited wealth; Hyman abbreviates this as much gold and a gift of silver and gold. Later, love of Torah enters Yose, and his teacher tells the rich man to give wealth to orphans and the poor; Yose returns the cup of paz. Hyman instead compresses the intervening event as a remarkable incident and says Yose distributed his wealth. His account, pronouns and ordering remain translated as his paraphrase, with these differences disclosed rather than silently harmonized. The cup, additional speeches, descendants and rewards are not inserted into the body. The exact Zohar printed folio and Sitrei Torah division and the separate Midrash ha-Ne’elam Genesis passage beginning “Let the earth bring forth” have not been independently collated. The earlier failed-request and other notes remain verbatim.
